etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English blome, from Old Norse blóm, from Proto-Germanic *blōmô (“flower”). Doublet of bloom (“spongy mass of metal”); see there for more.

definitions.definition: A blossom; the flower of a plant; an expanded bud.

quote.citation: 1843, William H[ickling] Prescott, History of the Conquest of Mexico, […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), New York, N.Y.: Harper and Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: the rich blooms and enamelled vegetation of the tropics

definitions.definition: (collective) Flowers.
(uncountable) The opening of flowers in general; the state of blossoming or of having the flowers open.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book III”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto II:
quote.text: O, not for thee the glow, the bloom,⁠Who changest not in any gale,⁠Nor branding summer suns availTo touch thy thousand years of gloom: […]

definitions.definition: (figuratively) A state or time of beauty, freshness, and vigor; an opening to higher perfection, analogous to that of buds into blossoms.

quote.citation: 1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne, The Scarlet Letter, a Romance, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, →OCLC:
quote.text: every successive mother had transmitted to her child a fainter bloom, a more delicate and briefer beauty.

quote.citation: 1992, “In Bloom”, in Kurt Cobain (lyrics), Nevermind, performed by Nirvana:
quote.text: We can have some more / Nature is a whore / Bruises on the fruit / Tender age in bloom

definitions.definition: Rosy colour; the flush or glow on a person's cheek.
The delicate, powdery coating upon certain growing or newly-gathered fruits or leaves, as on grapes, plums, etc.

quote.text: The bloom on blueberries is the dusty powder that protects them from the Sun; it does not rinse off.

definitions.definition: Anything giving an appearance of attractive freshness.

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 2, in Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: a new, fresh, brilliant world, with all the bloom upon it

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable) An algal bloom.

quote.citation: 2018, Tim Flannery, Europe: A Natural History, page 28:
quote.text: Where upwellings or other sources of nutrients allow Ehux to abound, it can proliferate, as blooms, to the point that the ocean turns milky.

definitions.definition: The clouded appearance which varnish sometimes takes upon the surface of a picture.
A yellowish deposit or powdery coating which appears on well-tanned leather.[1]
(mineralogy) A bright-hued variety of some minerals.
(cooking) A white area of cocoa butter that forms on the surface of chocolate when warmed and cooled.
A natural protective coating on an eggshell.
(television) An undesirable halo effect that may occur when a very bright region is displayed next to a very dark region of the screen.
(video games) The increase in bullet spread over time as a gun's trigger is kept held.

quote.citation: 2018 February 21, “Bullet Bloom: An FPS Tragedy”, in CritPoints‎[1]:
quote.text: Bloom does add a skill element, burst firing the weapon instead of holding the trigger down, but it's questionable if adding a skill element like that is the actual intent of bloom, because that’s a pretty lame and linear skill element to add, requiring people to tap the button instead of hold it down.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bloom (“a blossom”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to blossom; to make flourish.

quote.citation: 1594–1597, Richard Hooker, edited by J[ohn] S[penser], Of the Lawes of Ecclesiastical Politie, […], London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby [for Matthew Lownes], published 1611, →OCLC, (please specify the page):

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bestow a bloom upon; to make blooming or radiant.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book IV”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: The Tree of Life […] blooming Ambrosial Fruit Of vegetable Gold.

quote.citation: 1819 September 19, John Keats, “To Autumn”, in Lamia, Isabella, the Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems, London:  […]  [Thomas Davison] for Taylor and Hessey, […], published 1820, →OCLC, stanza 3, page 138:
quote.text: Where are the songs of Spring? Ay, where are they? / Think not of them, thou hast thy music too,— / While barred clouds bloom the soft-dying day, / And touch the stubble-plains with rosy hue; [...]

definitions.definition: (intransitive) Of a plant, to produce blooms; to open its blooms.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: A flower which once / In Paradise, fast by the tree of life, / Began to bloom.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, figuratively) To spread; to slowly expand like a field of flowers that blossom in fits and spurts.
(intransitive, figuratively) Of a person, business, etc, to flourish; to be in a state of healthful, growing youth and vigour; to show beauty and freshness.

quote.citation: 1961 November 10, Joseph Heller, “The Soldier in White”, in Catch-22 […], New York, N.Y.: Simon and Schuster, →OCLC, page 171:
quote.text: Nurse Cramer had a cute nose and a radiant, blooming complexion dotted with fetching sprays of adorable freckles that Yossarian detested.

quote.citation: 2017 May 13, Barney Ronay, “Antonio Conte’s brilliance has turned Chelsea’s pop-up team into champions”, in the Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: The attacking three have also been allowed to bloom. Liberated from deep defensive duties Eden Hazard has become more expressive, more obviously, flashily complete.
A better country blooms to view, / Beneath a brighter sky.

definitions.definition: (cooking) To bring out the flavor of a spice by cooking it in oil.
(intransitive, cooking, of chocolate) To develop a layer of bloom (white, spotty areas of cocoa butter) due to repeated warming and cooling.
(cooking) To let carbon dioxide to escape from coffee in order to improve the taste.
(cooking) To hydrate ingredients (such as gelatin or yeast) before using them.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English blome, from Old English blōma (“flower; lump of metal”), from Proto-Germanic *blōmô (“flower”). Cognate with West Frisian blom, Dutch bloem, German Blume, Icelandic blóm, Danish blomme, Gothic 𐌱𐌻𐍉𐌼𐌰 (blōma). Related to blow, blade, blead; also related to flower, foil, and belladonna.

definitions.definition: The spongy mass of metal formed in a furnace by the smelting process.

quote.citation: 1957, H.R. Schubert, History of the British Iron and Steel Industry, page 26:
quote.text: These metallic bodies gradually increasing in volume finally conglomerate into a larger mass, the bloom, which is extracted from the furnace with tongs.
